name: Straight-arm pulldown / pullover
angleNote: Shoulder flexion: 170° = arm overhead (start), 0° = arm by your side (end). Lifting makes the angle smaller.
jointNote: Not truly one joint: the shoulder blade turns upwards on the rib cage as the arm rises, so the angle here is the whole arm against the trunk. In 12 people reaching overhead, the shoulder joint itself moved about 2.3° for every 1° of shoulder-blade rotation on the way up (2.7 on the way down), and the first 30° came mostly from the shoulder joint (about 3.7 : 1); Inman's classic figure is 2 : 1. Pulling the arm down from overhead reverses this: the shoulder blade turns back down (lats, pecs and the lower trapezius) as well as the arm moving at the shoulder joint. The model treats the arm as turning about one fixed shoulder point; the shoulder-blade muscles (trapezius, serratus anterior) that turn the blade aren't analysed.
jointNoteSource: Braman JP, Engel SC, LaPrade RF, Ludewig PM (2009). In vivo assessment of scapulohumeral rhythm during unconstrained overhead reaching in asymptomatic subjects. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 18(6):960–967. doi:10.1016/j.jse.2009.02.001

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The forearm segment includes the hand (combined centre of mass along elbow → grip).
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Shoulder→elbow and elbow→grip centre in metres. The arm is modelled straight.

strengthCurve.label: Shoulder extensor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative shoulder-extension strength vs shoulder flexion: nearly flat, peaking around 65–100°. Clarke et al. (64 men, via Kulig et al.) measured 347 N at 65° and 262 N at 180°, varying by only 25.5 N between 45° and 135°; two other studies agree. The 0° value is an estimate (the curves rise from there). Mayer et al. place the isometric peak at 53–91°. Peak torque default: Mayer's isometric shoulder extension, men, 93 ± 24 Nm.
strengthCurve.source: Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (Clarke et al. data); Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25. doi:10.1055/s-2007-1021105

muscles.name: Latissimus dorsi
muscles.note: Main shoulder extensor; strongest pull with the arm high.

muscles.name: Triceps (long head)
muscles.note: Crosses the shoulder and helps extend it; also keeps the elbow straight.

muscles.name: Pectoralis major (sternal head)
muscles.note: Helps pull the arm down from overhead, mainly in the upper range.

phases.name: Finish
phases.text: Arm by your side. A high cable still pulls forward here; a lying dumbbell does not load this part at all.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: Arm in front. Cable torque is near its peak; a lying dumbbell only starts to load the arm once it passes vertical (90°).

phases.name: Overhead
phases.text: Arm overhead and lats stretched. The pullover is hardest here; a cable from in front loses its moment arm once your hand passes the pulley line.

variants.name: Cable straight-arm pulldown
variants.notes: Standing upright facing a high pulley (the usual slight forward lean isn't modelled). Tension is high through the middle and bottom of the pull; above the pulley line the cable stops resisting.

variants.name: Lying dumbbell pullover
variants.notes: Lying on your back, gravity points to your back: torque = −m·g·L·cos(angle). Zero with the arm vertical, largest overhead; below vertical the weight falls forward on its own.
